title: Arp 271: galaxies drawn together
caption: The interacting galaxies Arp 271, imaged by the New Technology Telescope

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Two spiral galaxies of similar size, NGC 5426 and NGC 5427, are caught in a slow gravitational encounter, linked by a bridge of stars that already joins them. Together they are known as Arp 271.

The two galaxies have already been changed by their meeting, although it is not certain that they will go on to collide and merge. The encounter will last for tens of millions of years, and their mutual pull will trigger the birth of new stars along the way. The bridge of stars between them is a visible sign of that pull.

Arp 271 lies 90 million light-years away toward the constellation Virgo (the Virgin) and spans about 130 000 light-years. William Herschel first discovered it in 1785. Our own Milky Way may go through a similar collision with the neighboring Andromeda galaxy in about five billion years. Andromeda is now about 2.6 million light-years away.

understand.summary: The EFOSC instrument on ESO's 3.58-meter New Technology Telescope recorded Arp 271 in visible light through B, V and R filters. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: A total exposure time of 4440 seconds gathers far more light than the eye can, so the faint bridge of stars shows up.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile is home to the 3.58-meter New Technology Telescope, and its EFOSC instrument took the picture. Data were collected through B, V and R filters for a total exposure time of 4440 seconds, and the field of view is about 4 arcminutes.
alt: Two similar spiral galaxies side by side, joined by a bridge of stars.
